value: Anyone licensed with your organisation or enterprise (not only members) who had a commit pushed to an enabled repository in the last 90 days.
reason: “Licensed member” leaves out external collaborators and pending invitees, whom the source counts as active committers.

value: A partner-program provider’s token leaks in a public repository where secret scanning alerts for users have not been enabled. The maintainer sees nothing in the Security and quality tab. Why?
reason: Secret scanning runs automatically on public repositories, so user alerts could appear; the front must rule them out for D to be the only answer.

value: B: partner scanning of public repositories runs whatever the repository settings, and cannot be reconfigured. C: historical scans are not the reason partner alerts are hidden. A: all branches are scanned.
reason: Matches the clarified front; source: “You cannot change the configuration of secret scanning for partner patterns on public repositories.”

value:
A) A repository administrator
B) A security manager
C) An enterprise owner who does not administer that repository
D) A user with a custom role with read/write access
reason: An organisation owner has admin access to every repository in the organisation (taught in github-foundations), so “an organisation owner who does not administer that repository” cannot exist.

value: C) An enterprise owner who does not administer that repository
Enterprise owners, like organisation owners, are notified only if they administer the repository where the secret leaked.
reason: Follows the corrected choice C; source: “Organization owners and enterprise owners, if they are administrators of repositories where secrets were leaked”.

value: A secret pasted into a discussion, a wiki page or a secret gist can be caught, not only one committed to code.
reason: Secret gists are not repository content, so “anywhere in the repository’s collaboration content” misdescribes them.

value: To review generic alerts across repositories, open security overview’s “Secret scanning” view, because the summary views leave them out.
reason: “Summary views therefore undercount if you expect generic alerts in them” is hard to parse.

value: Push protection blocks your push because the same key appears in your last three commits, first added in the oldest of them. Which approach removes it?
reason: “the oldest two commits back” reads two ways.

value: A protected repository already has open alerts for 1,200 secrets. A team pushes a branch whose history contains all 1,200 of them. Why is the push not blocked?
reason: “Existing secrets” are ones with alerts already created; alerts in an old, imported repository do not make them existing in the new one.

value: A is wrong: the Docs set no rule about imported history; the 1,000-secret limit is what applies here. D is wrong: the 50-megabyte limit is for public repositories, and nothing says this push is that large. C is wrong: the five-secret limit is about how many are shown, not whether the push is blocked.
reason: “A is not stated in the Docs” does not say why A is wrong.

value: Which type of push protection matches each description: (1) on by default for your account; (2) needs GitHub Secret Protection; (3) blocks pushes to one organisation’s private repositories?
reason: The front asks “Which type is each” twice.

value: The Docs say exemptions should go to trusted automation that pushes frequent commits with minimal friction.
reason: “The Docs meant exemptions for” is ungrammatical.

value: The limit is on how many secrets are shown at one time, not on how many are detected.
reason: “You see the rest only after dealing with those” is not in the source.

value: D: Expired, because reviewers have 7 days.
reason: The back (“It has expired”) did not match the wording of choice D.

value: A is wrong: the approval also covers future commits that contain the same secret. C is wrong: the three-hour window belongs to allowing a secret on the bypass page, not to an approved request. D is wrong: the Docs describe no alert being reopened; the approval simply lets the commit through.
reason: “D is not stated anywhere in the Docs” does not explain why D is wrong.

value: Like giving a post-room scanner the shape of your own company’s keys: tokens that start `acme_live_` become findable.
reason: Adding your own badge format to a list of forged passes suggests your real badges would be treated as forgeries.
